newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission set to adopt tobacco reform proposals.
newsitem.headline: Commission set to adopt tobacco reform proposals.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to propose on Wednesday new actions the European Union could take to discourage smoking while also reforming its controversial tobacco subsidy programme.
The Commission is not expected to endorse any radical measures such as an end to tobacco subsidies or restrictive anti-smoking legislation, EU sources said.
Thousands of EU tobacco farmers demonstrated outside the Commission headquarters on Wednesday, expressing concern about possible job losses.

The Commission is set to outline a series of options the EU should consider as it tries to cut down on the EU's half million annual smoking-related deaths -- for example, strengthening cigarette label warnings and reducing the tar and nicotine content of cigarettes.

It is also likely to endorse proposals by Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler to retarget tobacco subsidies to higher-quality products, offer buyouts to entice farmers away from tobacco and double the one percent levy on tobacco subsidies that is used to finance an EU tobacco public health fund, EU sources said.

Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn and three other commissioners -- Neil Kinnock, Anita Gradin and Karel Van Miert -- are still pushing for even deeper reforms, however, and the proposals could be put to a vote, they said.

Flynn, who argues the EU compromises its public health campaign by channeling more than $1 billion a year to tobacco growers, would like the Commission to agree on Wednesday to consider phasing out the subsidies in the long run, they said.

Fischler has so far rejected that solution, arguing that ending the subsidies would put some 200,000 tobacco growers and related workers out of jobs without cutting consumption since consumers would simply turn to imported products.
Eight EU countries, led by Italy and Greece, produce tobacco, much of it low quality.

The Commission is set to adopt without controversy the other, mostly low-key set of proposals on tobacco consumption. They would supplement the Commission's so-far unsuccessful effort to get EU states to ban all tobacco advertising.
A draft paper drawn up by Flynn says the EU should, for example, consider declaring nicotine addiction a "dependency," thus allowing it to be tackled by EU public health programmes.
It should also consider amending EU rules to lower the maximum tar content of cigarettes and set a maximum nicotine content level.

Other options listed by the paper, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, include adopting EU rules on additives in tobacco products, setting up a tobacco consumption monitoring system, agreeing a code of practice on children's right to a smoke-free environment and promoting public health studies.
It also suggests reviewing EU labelling rules to see whether health warnings could be improved and defining "light" and "low" tobacco products so they do not mislead consumers.
